query: FeCoNi is an fcc alloy with high saturation magnetization and a low coercive field. Earlier studies examined the high-entropy alloys FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt, but both exhibited soft ferromagnetism. A qualifying high-entropy alloy must have an almost equiatomic multicomponent composition and configurational entropy of at least 1.0R. Subject to these constraints, what single intervention could produce a FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy with greater coercivity than the prior derivatives? Present one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an appropriate FeCoNi-based baseline, defines the conditions over which it should apply, cites supporting observations from earlier work, and proposes a discriminating experiment with an explicit falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Rapid quenching of an as‐cast, nearly equiatomic FeCoNiTi high-entropy alloy stabilizes a dual-phase microstructure (ferromagnetic fcc and hexagonal C14 Laves phases) that enhances the coercive field compared to single-phase fcc alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast high-entropy alloy FeCoNiTi (nominal 1:1:1:1) containing dual phases; an fcc phase and a hexagonal C14 Laves phase with characteristic chemical segregations.
generation.intervention: Apply rapid quenching via arc melting on a water-cooled Cu hearth to lock in the dual-phase microstructure. In parallel, synthesize a compositionally matched C14-dominant variant (Fe27Co27Ni17Ti29) for controlled comparison.
generation.conditions: Perform magnetic measurements up to 400 K and use spin-polarized density of states calculations under similar synthesis conditions to ensure consistent composition and phase evolution.
generation.structural_mediator: The microstructure featuring a ferromagnetic fcc phase (approximate composition: 21.3% Fe–24.8% Co–32.2% Ni–21.6% Ti) coexisting with a C14 Laves phase (approximate composition: 27.3% Fe–26.6% Co–17.4% Ni–28.7% Ti) mediates the effects via phase boundaries and chemical segregation.
generation.mechanism: Antiferromagnetic coupling between the Fe/Co/Ni sublattice and the Ti sublattice in the fcc phase reduces the overall saturation magnetization but enhances orbital contributions. In the presence of the C14 phase and potential spin canting, domain wall pinning is promoted, leading to a marked increase in coercivity. The distinct magnetic ordering temperatures (with the fcc phase ordering around 1084 K and showing transitions at about 168 K, and the C14 phase contributing a lower temperature transition near 214 K) further support a dual-phase-mediated enhancement.
generation.predicted_outcome: The dual-phase FeCoNiTi alloy is predicted to exhibit a coercive field around 667 Oe at 400 K, significantly above the <100 Oe observed in single-phase fcc FeCoNi high-entropy alloys. Multiple, distinct magnetic ordering temperatures should be observed, marking the presence of both phases.
generation.baseline: Single-phase fcc FeCoNi high-entropy alloys that typically exhibit coercivity less than 100 Oe and limited contribution from orbital moments.
generation.boundary: The enhanced coercivity arises from the coexistence and interfacial interactions between the fcc and C14 phases. If rapid quenching does not stabilize the dual-phase microstructure (or if the composition deviates so that only a single phase forms), the predicted enhancement will not occur.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the exact magnitude of the coercivity enhancement, as it may depend on fine differences in phase fraction and interface quality. Reproducibility across different synthesis batches may also vary.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize the rapid-quenched dual-phase FeCoNiTi alloy alongside a compositionally matched C14-dominant alloy (Fe27Co27Ni17Ti29). Measure the coercive fields and temperature-dependent magnetization to identify distinct magnetic transition temperatures.
measurements: Vibrating sample magnetometry (VSM) to determine the coercive field at temperatures up to 400 K.
Temperature-dependent magnetization measurements to detect magnetic ordering transitions (targeting transitions near 1084 K, 168 K, and 214 K).
Phase identification via X-ray diffraction (XRD) to verify the coexistence of fcc and C14 phases.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the dual-phase FeCoNiTi alloy does not exhibit a coercivity significantly greater than 100 Oe (and ideally around 667 Oe at 400 K), or if the magnetic ordering temperatures do not match the predicted distinct transitions (with the absence or merging of the expected fcc and C14 features), then the hypothesis is rejected.
